findings.title: Monotonic clock is execution-local
findings.description: The monotonic clock cannot compare events across executions.

evidence.quote: The monotonic clock only exists within a single execution of the user agent, so it can’t be used to compare events that might happen in different executions.

findings.machine_interpretation: Monotonic time is not comparable across executions.
findings.scope_rationale: This matters to time assurance because monotonicity bounds are execution-local.

findings.title: Durations are clock-agnostic
findings.description: Durations calculated on one clock may be applied to another.

evidence.quote: Since all clocks attempt to count at the same rate, durations don’t have an associated clock, and a duration calculated from two moments on one clock can be added to a moment from a second clock

findings.machine_interpretation: Duration values are treated as clock-independent.
findings.scope_rationale: This matters to time assurance because cross-clock duration reuse can hide clock discontinuities.

findings.title: Expiry uses wall-clock comparison
findings.description: Reporting depends on wall-clock comparison against an expiry offset.

evidence.quote: If context’s current wall time is less than source’s source time + source’s expiry, send a report.

findings.machine_interpretation: Expiry decision is a wall-time inequality.
findings.scope_rationale: This matters to time assurance because wall-clock skew changes expiry outcomes.
